screens.title: Understanding and Implementing Logical Volume Management (LVM)
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn why LVM matters and how it changes the way you manage disk space. LVM removes the rigid coupling between physical disks and filesystems by introducing three layers: physical volumes, volume groups, and logical volumes. That layering means you can combine multiple disks into a single flexible pool, carve out resizable logical volumes, and grow storage for a live filesystem in many cases without downtime. Practically, you will initialize disks with pvcreate, aggregate them into a VG with vgcreate, make LVs with lvcreate, and grow both the LV and its filesystem using lvextend and xfs_growfs or resize2fs. A short hands-on scenario in this chapter walks through creating PVs on two new virtual disks, building vg_data, creating lv_web, formatting it, mounting it, and later extending it. We also highlight common mistakes to avoid, like forgetting to resize the filesystem after lvextend. By the end, you should feel confident creating an LVM stack, verifying each layer, and safely expanding storage when needed. Would you like to try a hands-on setup after this overview?

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Understanding and Implementing LVM
Logical Volume Management (LVM)
Pool disks, carve resizable volumes, and grow filesystems safely

LVM introduces three layers: Physical Volumes (PVs), Volume Groups (VGs), and Logical Volumes (LVs). Use pvcreate to initialize disks, vgcreate to pool them, and lvcreate to allocate space. For many filesystems you can extend an LV and then expand the filesystem without downtime. This model is especially useful on servers where storage needs change often.

In this lesson
Core concepts, commands, a step-by-step lab and common mistakes to avoid.
Why it matters
Scale filesystems without repartitioning and reduce planned downtime for growth events.
Visual concept
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Physical Volumes
Disks or partitions initialized with pvcreate, e.g. /dev/sdb, /dev/sdc.
Volume Group
A pooled container that spans one or many PVs and supplies extents for LVs.
Logical Volume
A resizable block device you format and mount, for example /dev/vg_data/lv_web.
Explore Key Topics
Initialize PVs
pvcreate /dev/sdb
Make a VG
vgcreate vg_data /dev/sdb /dev/sdc
Create LV & Grow
lvcreate, lvextend, xfs_growfs
Coming up: a hands-on setup using two unpartitioned virtual disks and an extend example that highlights a common mistake.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain why LVM is used on Linux servers, initialize physical disks for LVM, create and manage volume groups, and allocate logical volumes for filesystems. First, you will describe the LVM hierarchy — PV, VG, LV — and why pooling storage simplifies growth. Second, you'll practice commands to create physical volumes and verify them, which matters because an uninitialized disk won't be usable by LVM. Third, you'll combine PVs into a volume group and create logical volumes, format them, and mount them for real use. Finally, you'll extend logical volumes and then resize their filesystems so the OS can see the new space. Each objective includes a practical skill and the reason it matters in operations: avoiding downtime, simplifying storage reallocation, and preventing common mistakes such as forgetting to resize the filesystem after an lvextend. We'll verify competency with a milestone at the end of the hands-on activity where you successfully extend an LV and confirm the filesystem shows the new size.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Lab & Verification
Verification checklist
Commands you will use during the lab and what they tell you.
pvcreate / pvs
Initialize disks and list PVs to confirm size and UUIDs.
vgcreate / vgs
Create VG and check free extents before allocating LVs.
lvcreate / lvs
Create LVs and confirm their device names and sizes.
Check filesystem
Use df -h to confirm mount size and verify changes after grow operations.
Common mistake
Extending an LV alone does not resize the filesystem. You must run the appropriate grow tool for the filesystem type.

screens.title: What LVM is and why it's used
screens.narratorSegment: Logical Volume Management is a storage abstraction layer that sits above physical disks and partitions. At its core, LVM lets you treat one or more disks as a single logical pool, then create logical volumes inside that pool. The immediate benefit is flexibility: you can allocate, extend, or sometimes relocate volumes without repartitioning physical disks. A concrete example is combining two small virtual disks into one volume group and creating a single logical volume that presents as a single filesystem to applications. This avoids the headache of juggling multiple mount points or resizing physical partitions. A common misconception is that LVM automatically provides redundancy; it does not. LVM provides flexible allocation and growth, but you still need RAID or other redundancy mechanisms for fault tolerance. Another important point is that while many operations can happen online, filesystem compatibility matters. For example, XFS supports online growth with xfs_growfs, while some filesystems may have additional constraints. As you learn commands and practice the hands-on lab, keep the distinction clear: LVM manages block devices, and filesystems live on top of those block devices and must be resized separately. How would you combine multiple small disks into one pool when you need a contiguous logical space?

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › What LVM is
Definition and purpose
LVM pools disks and provides resizable logical volumes for filesystems.
• LVM abstracts physical storage so you can treat many disks as a single pool.
• Logical volumes behave like partitions but can be extended or moved more flexibly.
• LVM itself is not a backup or redundancy solution; pair it with RAID if you need fault tolerance.
Analogy: Think of PVs as bricks, a VG as the wall, and LVs as rooms carved from that wall. Rooms can be expanded by adding more bricks to the wall.
Concrete example
You have /dev/sdb (2GB) and /dev/sdc (3GB). Initialize them as PVs, create vg_data, then create lv_web of 2GB. Mount and use it as a single filesystem without partitioning a larger disk.
Key takeaway
LVM adds a flexible layer between disks and filesystems, making growth and reallocation easier.

screens.title: LVM hierarchy: PV → VG → LV
screens.narratorSegment: LVM's structure is simple but important: Physical Volumes, Volume Groups, and Logical Volumes. A Physical Volume is a disk or partition prepared with pvcreate. Multiple PVs combine into a Volume Group, which represents a pool of storage from which Logical Volumes are allocated. Logical Volumes are the usable block devices you format with a filesystem and mount. One additional concept is the extent: the smallest allocation unit LVM uses inside a VG. Extents let LVM track allocation granularity; when you request space for an LV, LVM assigns one or more extents. For example, a VG might have many 4MB extents and a free pool of several extents. When you create an LV, you request a number of extents or a size that LVM converts to extents. A common confusion is treating PVs like filesystems — they are not. PVs are raw, low-level objects that LVM manages. Also remember that while you can often grow an LV if the VG has free extents, you cannot grow beyond what the VG contains. Keep this relationship in mind when planning capacity. How many extents would you need for a 10GB LV if your VG uses 4MB extents?

keyIdea.title: Three layers and extents
keyIdea.text: PVs supply extents to a VG; LVs consume extents. Planning extents determines how granular growth will be.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › LVM Hierarchy
The LVM stack
How PV, VG, LV and extents relate and why each layer exists.
Physical Volume (PV)
A disk or partition prepared with pvcreate. It contributes physical space to a VG.
Volume Group (VG)
A pool of storage made from one or more PVs. It tracks free extents for allocation.
Logical Volume (LV)
Allocations taken from the VG. Format with a filesystem to make them usable.
Extent concept
Extents are the smallest LVM allocation units inside a VG. They determine how finely you can grow or shrink LVs. Remember: LVs consume extents and cannot exceed the VG's free extents.
Misconception
PVs are not filesystems and adding a PV does not automatically change mounted filesystems — you must create or extend LVs and filesystems explicitly.
Check your understanding
If a VG has 5GB free and you need a 6GB LV, what step must you take before creating the LV? (Answer: add another PV to the VG to supply the extra extents.)

screens.title: Initializing Physical Volumes with pvcreate
screens.narratorSegment: Initializing physical volumes is the first hands-on step. The pvcreate command marks a disk or partition for use by LVM. A common example in this chapter is initializing two unpartitioned disks: /dev/sdb and /dev/sdc. Running pvcreate writes metadata so LVM can track the PV. After pvcreate, use pvs or pvdisplay to confirm initialization and view size and UUIDs. A useful habit is to check for mounted filesystems or existing signatures before initializing, because pvcreate will overwrite existing partition or filesystem metadata on the device. For example, a cautious admin would run file system detection tools or lsblk to confirm the device is unused. Concrete command sequence from the lab: sudo pvcreate /dev/sdb /dev/sdc, then sudo pvs to verify. Misconception to avoid: pvcreate does not create filesystems or mount points — it only prepares block devices for LVM. Finish by reflecting: what would you check on a new disk before running pvcreate to avoid accidental data loss? Initializing Physical Volumes with pvcreate means pvcreate writes lvm metadata to a disk or partition; always verify the device is unused before initializing.. In practical terms, commands to prepare raw disks or partitions for lvm. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › pvcreate
Prepare disks for LVM
Use pvcreate to initialize raw disks or partitions so LVM can manage them.
Key commands
sudo pvcreate /dev/sdb /dev/sdc
sudo pvs
sudo pvdisplay
Example and checks
Example: initialize two new virtual disks for a demo. After pvcreate, run pvs to confirm the PVs appear and show expected sizes. If a disk contained data, pvcreate would overwrite its metadata, so always verify first.
Misconception
pvcreate does not preserve existing filesystems. It prepares the device for LVM metadata only.
Pro tip
Run lsblk and blkid to confirm a device is not in use before running pvcreate to avoid data loss.

screens.title: Creating and extending Volume Groups
screens.narratorSegment: A Volume Group combines one or more physical volumes into a single pool from which logical volumes draw storage. You create a VG using vgcreate and list or inspect it with vgs or vgdisplay. In the lab, creating vg_data from /dev/sdb and /dev/sdc gives you a single pool for lv_web. If you need more capacity later, add another PV to the system with pvcreate and then run vgextend to add that PV into the existing VG. This increases the VG's free extents and enables larger LVs or more LVs overall. A common error is to assume vgcreate copies data — it only aggregates devices. Always check vgs to confirm available free space before creating or extending LVs. Concrete commands: sudo vgcreate vg_data /dev/sdb /dev/sdc, sudo vgs to view free extents, later sudo pvcreate /dev/sdd and sudo vgextend vg_data /dev/sdd to grow the pool. Why it matters: a thoughtful VG layout lets you scale capacity smoothly without disrupting existing LVs. After vgextend, what command will you run to confirm the VG now has more free extents? Creating and extending Volume Groups means use vgcreate to combine pvs and vgextend to add more physical devices when you need capacity.. In practical terms, vgcreate to build pools and vgextend to add capacity later. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › VG Workflow
Create and grow a Volume Group
Commands and checks to combine PVs and add capacity later.
Create VG
sudo vgcreate vg_data /dev/sdb /dev/sdc
sudo vgs
sudo vgdisplay vg_data
Extend VG
# After pvcreate /dev/sdd
sudo vgextend vg_data /dev/sdd
sudo vgs
Why this matters
VGs let you decouple physical growth from logical allocation; you can add disks later without touching existing LVs.
Common mistake
Forgetting to run vgs or vgdisplay after vgextend can leave you unaware of free extents available for new LVs.
Check question
After vgextend, run vgs. What field tells you how much free space is available for new LVs? (Answer: VFree or VSize/VFree columns.)

screens.title: Creating Logical Volumes, formatting and mounting
screens.narratorSegment: Once you have a VG, create Logical Volumes which act like partitions. Use lvcreate to allocate space from the VG; for instance sudo lvcreate -L 2G -n lv_web vg_data creates a 2GB LV named lv_web inside vg_data. The LV appears as a block device, typically under /dev/vg_data/lv_web. Next, format the LV with a filesystem such as ext4 or XFS. Example: sudo mkfs. ext4 /dev/vg_data/lv_web. Then create a mount point and mount the LV so applications can use it. Example: sudo mkdir -p /var/www/html && sudo mount /dev/vg_data/lv_web /var/www/html. Verify with df -h to see the mounted size. A frequent misconception is thinking lvcreate also formats the LV — it does not. Formatting and mounting are separate steps. Always verify the LV device path exists under /dev and confirm the filesystem type after mkfs. Closing question: after creating lv_web and mounting it, what command will show the device and its mount point? Creating Logical Volumes, formatting and mounting means create the lv, format it with mkfs, mount it, and confirm the filesystem with df -h.. In practical terms, lvcreate, mkfs, and mount to make storage available. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Create the LV, format it with mkfs, mount it, and confirm the filesystem with df -h.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Create & Mount LV
Allocate an LV and make it usable
Commands to create lv_web, format as ext4, and mount.
sudo lvcreate -L 2G -n lv_web vg_data
sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/vg_data/lv_web
sudo mkdir -p /var/www/html
sudo mount /dev/vg_data/lv_web /var/www/html
df -h /var/www/html
Checks and notes
After lvcreate, confirm the device appears in /dev and lvs output. mkfs creates the filesystem; mount makes it accessible. Use df -h to confirm the size shown by the filesystem matches the LV size.
Example
In the lab, lv_web of 2GB was formatted ext4 and mounted to /var/www/html for web content storage.
Misconception
lvcreate does not imply a filesystem exists; you must run mkfs and mount separately.

screens.title: Extending a Logical Volume with lvextend
screens.narratorSegment: Extending a logical volume is a two-step idea: allocate more block space to the LV, then resize the filesystem so it can use the added space. First, confirm your VG has free extents with vgs or vgdisplay. If vg_data has free space, run sudo lvextend -L +1G /dev/vg_data/lv_web to add one gigabyte. Alternatively, use -l +100%FREE to allocate all remaining space. After lvextend, the LV device is larger, but the mounted filesystem still reports the old size until you grow it. For XFS, use sudo xfs_growfs /mnt/point (or the LV device) while it is mounted. For ext4, use sudo resize2fs /dev/vg_data/lv_web; ext4 can often be grown while mounted too. A common mistake is running resize before lvextend or forgetting to check VG free space first, which leads to errors. Example lab steps: lvextend -L +1G /dev/vg_data/lv_web, sudo lvs to verify LV size, then resize2fs /dev/vg_data/lv_web and df -h /var/www/html to confirm. What would you do if lvextend fails due to insufficient VG space? Extending a Logical Volume with lvextend means lvextend increases the block device size; a separate filesystem grow command makes the new space usable.. In practical terms, grow an lv when the vg has free space. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

narration.text: Extending a logical volume is a two-step idea: allocate more block space to the LV, then resize the filesystem so it can use the added space. First, confirm your VG has free extents with vgs or vgdisplay. If vg_data has free space, run sudo lvextend -L +1G /dev/vg_data/lv_web to add one gigabyte. A common mistake is running resize before lvextend or forgetting to check VG free space first, which leads to errors. If you forget the filesystem step, df -h will not reflect the new space even though the LV size changed. screens.title: Extent allocation and planning capacity
screens.narratorSegment: Extents are the atomic allocation units inside a volume group. When you create a VG, LVM chooses an extent size (often 4 MB by default) which controls the smallest chunk of space an LV can consume. Planning extents matters when you need predictable growth granularity: small extents let you allocate finer increments, while larger extents may reduce metadata overhead but increase wasted space. In practice, you rarely change extent size after creating a VG, so choose it with future growth in mind. Use vgs to view available free extents and lvs to inspect LV allocation. A concrete scenario: a VG with 4MB extents needs roughly 2560 extents to represent 10GB. A common oversight is trying to create an LV larger than the VG's free extents; the command will fail. To resolve that, add a PV and vgextend the VG, or reduce the requested LV size. Key takeaway: plan VG capacity, choose sensible extent sizes, and verify free extents before allocating large LVs. screens.title: Shrinking LVs: risks and safer alternatives
screens.narratorSegment: Shrinking logical volumes is possible but risky and more complex than growing them. To shrink an LV safely, you typically must shrink the filesystem first, which often requires unmounting it or booting into rescue mode. For ext4, you must reduce the filesystem size before reducing the LV size. For XFS, shrinking is generally unsupported; you must back up data, recreate the filesystem on a smaller LV, and restore data. Because of these complications, many administrators prefer adding new LVs, migrating services, or expanding storage instead of shrinking existing volumes. A practical alternative is to create a new LV where needed and move data to it, or add another PV to the VG and rebalance. Always ensure you have a verified backup before attempting any shrink operation. Common misconception: shrinking is a simple reverse of growing. It is not. It requires strict ordering, backups, and sometimes offline maintenance. If you need to free space, can you plan an approach that avoids shrinking? Why shrinking is riskier than growing
Shrinking requires filesystem reductions and often offline steps; errors can cause data loss.
Risk checklist
• Backup data before any shrink operation. • Unmount or use rescue mode to shrink filesystems safely. • XFS cannot be shrunk; plan a rebuild if necessary.
Safer alternatives

screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on walkthrough follows the lab scenario using two unpartitioned virtual disks, /dev/sdb (2GB) and /dev/sdc (3GB). fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn why LVM matters and how it changes the way you manage disk space. LVM removes the rigid coupling between physical disks and filesystems by introducing three layers: physical volumes, volume groups, and logical volumes. That layering means you can combine multiple disks into a single flexible pool, carve out resizable logical volumes, and grow storage for a live filesystem in many cases without downtime. Practically, you will initialize disks with pvcreate, aggregate them into a VG with vgcreate, make LVs with lvcreate, and grow both the LV and its filesystem using lvextend and xfs_growfs or resize2fs. A short hands-on scenario in this chapter walks through creating PVs on two new virtual disks, building vg_data, creating lv_web, formatting it, mounting it, and later extending it. We also highlight common mistakes to avoid, like forgetting to resize the filesystem after lvextend. By the end, you should feel confident creating an LVM stack, verifying each layer, and safely expanding storage when needed. Would you like to try a hands-on setup after this overview?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain why LVM is used on Linux servers, initialize physical disks for LVM, create and manage volume groups, and allocate logical volumes for filesystems. First, you will describe the LVM hierarchy — PV, VG, LV — and why pooling storage simplifies growth. Second, you'll practice commands to create physical volumes and verify them, which matters because an uninitialized disk won't be usable by LVM. Third, you'll combine PVs into a volume group and create logical volumes, format them, and mount them for real use. Finally, you'll extend logical volumes and then resize their filesystems so the OS can see the new space. Each objective includes a practical skill and the reason it matters in operations: avoiding downtime, simplifying storage reallocation, and preventing common mistakes such as forgetting to resize the filesystem after an lvextend. We'll verify competency with a milestone at the end of the hands-on activity where you successfully extend an LV and confirm the filesystem shows the new size.

This second objectives slide focuses on verification steps and the lab flow you will perform. You will run pvs, vgs, and lvs to inspect the current state after each change, and use mkfs and mount to make storage accessible. The verification matters because commands like lvextend change the block device but the filesystem remains the final authority on usable space. You will also practice checking df -h to confirm the mounted filesystem size before and after growing it. In the hands-on scenario we initialize two raw disks as PVs, create vg_data, allocate lv_web and format it ext4, then mount to /var/www/html. Later we extend lv_web and use resize2fs to grow the ext4 filesystem. The milestone is to run df -h and see the increased capacity. This objective reinforces command discipline: verify before and after every change to avoid surprises and to ensure recovery points exist.

Logical Volume Management is a storage abstraction layer that sits above physical disks and partitions. At its core, LVM lets you treat one or more disks as a single logical pool, then create logical volumes inside that pool. The immediate benefit is flexibility: you can allocate, extend, or sometimes relocate volumes without repartitioning physical disks. A concrete example is combining two small virtual disks into one volume group and creating a single logical volume that presents as a single filesystem to applications. This avoids the headache of juggling multiple mount points or resizing physical partitions. A common misconception is that LVM automatically provides redundancy; it does not. LVM provides flexible allocation and growth, but you still need RAID or other redundancy mechanisms for fault tolerance. Another important point is that while many operations can happen online, filesystem compatibility matters. For example, XFS supports online growth with xfs_growfs, while some filesystems may have additional constraints. As you learn commands and practice the hands-on lab, keep the distinction clear: LVM manages block devices, and filesystems live on top of those block devices and must be resized separately. How would you combine multiple small disks into one pool when you need a contiguous logical space?

LVM's structure is simple but important: Physical Volumes, Volume Groups, and Logical Volumes. A Physical Volume is a disk or partition prepared with pvcreate. Multiple PVs combine into a Volume Group, which represents a pool of storage from which Logical Volumes are allocated. Logical Volumes are the usable block devices you format with a filesystem and mount. One additional concept is the extent: the smallest allocation unit LVM uses inside a VG. Extents let LVM track allocation granularity; when you request space for an LV, LVM assigns one or more extents. For example, a VG might have many 4MB extents and a free pool of several extents. When you create an LV, you request a number of extents or a size that LVM converts to extents. A common confusion is treating PVs like filesystems — they are not. PVs are raw, low-level objects that LVM manages. Also remember that while you can often grow an LV if the VG has free extents, you cannot grow beyond what the VG contains. Keep this relationship in mind when planning capacity. How many extents would you need for a 10GB LV if your VG uses 4MB extents?

Initializing physical volumes is the first hands-on step. The pvcreate command marks a disk or partition for use by LVM. A common example in this chapter is initializing two unpartitioned disks: /dev/sdb and /dev/sdc. Running pvcreate writes metadata so LVM can track the PV. After pvcreate, use pvs or pvdisplay to confirm initialization and view size and UUIDs. A useful habit is to check for mounted filesystems or existing signatures before initializing, because pvcreate will overwrite existing partition or filesystem metadata on the device. For example, a cautious admin would run file system detection tools or lsblk to confirm the device is unused. Concrete command sequence from the lab: sudo pvcreate /dev/sdb /dev/sdc, then sudo pvs to verify. Misconception to avoid: pvcreate does not create filesystems or mount points — it only prepares block devices for LVM. Finish by reflecting: what would you check on a new disk before running pvcreate to avoid accidental data loss? Initializing Physical Volumes with pvcreate means pvcreate writes lvm metadata to a disk or partition; always verify the device is unused before initializing.. In practical terms, commands to prepare raw disks or partitions for lvm. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A Volume Group combines one or more physical volumes into a single pool from which logical volumes draw storage. You create a VG using vgcreate and list or inspect it with vgs or vgdisplay. In the lab, creating vg_data from /dev/sdb and /dev/sdc gives you a single pool for lv_web. If you need more capacity later, add another PV to the system with pvcreate and then run vgextend to add that PV into the existing VG. This increases the VG's free extents and enables larger LVs or more LVs overall. A common error is to assume vgcreate copies data — it only aggregates devices. Always check vgs to confirm available free space before creating or extending LVs. Concrete commands: sudo vgcreate vg_data /dev/sdb /dev/sdc, sudo vgs to view free extents, later sudo pvcreate /dev/sdd and sudo vgextend vg_data /dev/sdd to grow the pool. Why it matters: a thoughtful VG layout lets you scale capacity smoothly without disrupting existing LVs. After vgextend, what command will you run to confirm the VG now has more free extents? Once you have a VG, create Logical Volumes which act like partitions. Use lvcreate to allocate space from the VG; for instance sudo lvcreate -L 2G -n lv_web vg_data creates a 2GB LV named lv_web inside vg_data. The LV appears as a block device, typically under /dev/vg_data/lv_web. Next, format the LV with a filesystem such as ext4 or XFS. Example: sudo mkfs. ext4 /dev/vg_data/lv_web. Then create a mount point and mount the LV so applications can use it. Example: sudo mkdir -p /var/www/html && sudo mount /dev/vg_data/lv_web /var/www/html. Verify with df -h to see the mounted size. A frequent misconception is thinking lvcreate also formats the LV — it does not. Formatting and mounting are separate steps. Always verify the LV device path exists under /dev and confirm the filesystem type after mkfs. Closing question: after creating lv_web and mounting it, what command will show the device and its mount point? Creating Logical Volumes, formatting and mounting means create the lv, format it with mkfs, mount it, and confirm the filesystem with df -h.. Extending a logical volume is a two-step idea: allocate more block space to the LV, then resize the filesystem so it can use the added space. First, confirm your VG has free extents with vgs or vgdisplay. If vg_data has free space, run sudo lvextend -L +1G /dev/vg_data/lv_web to add one gigabyte. Alternatively, use -l +100%FREE to allocate all remaining space. After lvextend, the LV device is larger, but the mounted filesystem still reports the old size until you grow it. For XFS, use sudo xfs_growfs /mnt/point (or the LV device) while it is mounted. For ext4, use sudo resize2fs /dev/vg_data/lv_web; ext4 can often be grown while mounted too. A common mistake is running resize before lvextend or forgetting to check VG free space first, which leads to errors. Example lab steps: lvextend -L +1G /dev/vg_data/lv_web, sudo lvs to verify LV size, then resize2fs /dev/vg_data/lv_web and df -h /var/www/html to confirm. When you grow an LV, the filesystem type determines the correct grow command and behavior. XFS is commonly used on RHEL systems and supports online growth using xfs_growfs. After lvextend, run sudo xfs_growfs /mount/point to expand the XFS filesystem while it remains mounted. For ext4, the resize2fs command resizes ext4 filesystems; depending on kernel and tools, ext4 can often be extended while mounted, but the command targets the device rather than the mount point. A concrete example: after increasing lv_web by 1GB, run xfs_growfs /var/www/html for XFS or resize2fs /dev/vg_data/lv_web for ext4, then confirm with df -h. A misconception is assuming the same command works for both filesystems — it does not. Another practical note: always run lvextend first, then the filesystem grow command. If you forget the filesystem step, df -h will not reflect the new space even though the LV size changed. Extents are the atomic allocation units inside a volume group. When you create a VG, LVM chooses an extent size (often 4 MB by default) which controls the smallest chunk of space an LV can consume. Planning extents matters when you need predictable growth granularity: small extents let you allocate finer increments, while larger extents may reduce metadata overhead but increase wasted space. In practice, you rarely change extent size after creating a VG, so choose it with future growth in mind. Use vgs to view available free extents and lvs to inspect LV allocation. A concrete scenario: a VG with 4MB extents needs roughly 2560 extents to represent 10GB. A common oversight is trying to create an LV larger than the VG's free extents; the command will fail. To resolve that, add a PV and vgextend the VG, or reduce the requested LV size. Key takeaway: plan VG capacity, choose sensible extent sizes, and verify free extents before allocating large LVs. Shrinking logical volumes is possible but risky and more complex than growing them. To shrink an LV safely, you typically must shrink the filesystem first, which often requires unmounting it or booting into rescue mode. For ext4, you must reduce the filesystem size before reducing the LV size. For XFS, shrinking is generally unsupported; you must back up data, recreate the filesystem on a smaller LV, and restore data. Because of these complications, many administrators prefer adding new LVs, migrating services, or expanding storage instead of shrinking existing volumes. A practical alternative is to create a new LV where needed and move data to it, or add another PV to the VG and rebalance. Always ensure you have a verified backup before attempting any shrink operation. Common misconception: shrinking is a simple reverse of growing. It is not. It requires strict ordering, backups, and sometimes offline maintenance. If you need to free space, can you plan an approach that avoids shrinking? This hands-on walkthrough follows the lab scenario using two unpartitioned virtual disks, /dev/sdb (2GB) and /dev/sdc (3GB). First initialize both as PVs: sudo pvcreate /dev/sdb /dev/sdc, then verify with sudo pvs. Next create a VG called vg_data with sudo vgcreate vg_data /dev/sdb /dev/sdc and confirm with sudo vgs. Remember these three core ideas as you work with LVM. First, LVM is an abstraction: it pools physical disks into a volume group and exposes logical volumes for filesystems. Second, commands matter in sequence: pvcreate initializes devices, vgcreate and vgextend build and grow pools, lvcreate and lvextend allocate and expand LVs, and finally xfs_growfs or resize2fs grow filesystems so the OS can use new space. Third, exercise care with shrinking and verify every step using pvs, vgs, lvs, and df -h. A common operational rule is to prefer adding capacity rather than shrinking volumes unless you have tested recovery and backups. These three reminders will help you avoid data loss and operational surprises while using LVM in production or labs.
